What this demonstrates

Revenue is not cash. An order can have several items and payments. Joining them carelessly multiplies totals. A refund grant and its cash return must not both reduce revenue. MerchantOps makes those relationships explicit and tests the difficult cases.

What is connected?

This public demo uses synthetic data. The source includes an offline Shopify CSV adapter for a restricted paid-order profile, tested with synthetic fixtures. Real merchant exports, refunded or taxed orders, and a live Shopify connection are not verified or connected.

One refund. Counted once.

A SIX-STEP WORKED EXAMPLE

What are we checking? A January sale receives a refund in February. We check that the refund reduces sales once, importing it again does not duplicate it, and returning the money clears what is owed without reducing sales again.

This is a separate, tiny synthetic example—not the store totals above. The channel filter does not change it. “After the sale” is different from an old record arriving late; this walkthrough tests the former.

Contribution means sales after discounts and approved refunds, minus item costs, delivery, payment fees and advertising. It is not net profit: rent, salaries, tax and other overheads are excluded. We assume no recovered stock value or refunded costs in this example.

Which products need attention?
SKU RETURNS · ORDER DATE
Follows the channel filter. Any partial refund counts once as a refunded order; refund value uses charged revenue as its denominator. Merchandise contribution excludes order shipping, payment fees and ads; those costs are accounted for at order/channel level. Newer orders have less time to return.

Acquisition, with the denominator visible
FIRST OBSERVED ORDER
All channels shown for comparison. CAC = channel spend ÷ customers whose first observed order is in that channel. Same-day ties use order ID. Blended revenue/spend includes repeat orders; neither measure proves incremental acquisition.

Does the cash match the ledger?
PAYMENT RECONCILIATION
Captured and returned amounts include only successful payment events. A failed attempt creates no revenue or cash. “Refund payable” is a granted refund not yet matched by returned cash; it is an exception to investigate, not necessarily an error.

Source SQL used to build the numbers above. Product contribution excludes shared shipping, payment fees and advertising; no arbitrary SKU allocation is implied.
Monthly financial ledger · SQL
Metric contract & limitations
Gross merchandise value excludes tax. Revenue follows the sale date; payment captures and returns are reconciled separately. Successful payment fees are recognised on their event dates. Net revenue = gross − discounts − refunds. Contribution = net revenue − COGS − outbound shipping − payment fees − advertising. Costs and fees are not recovered on refund; inventory recovery, overhead, GST and reverse logistics are excluded. This is contribution, not net profit.
Refunds use processing date in monthly reporting. Product economics attach all loaded refunds to their original orders. Attribution is the order's recorded channel, not an incrementality claim. Data ends 30 June 2026.
